questions.prompt: What does subprocess let a Python program do?
options: Run external commands and capture their output
questions.explanation: It is the bridge between Python and the command line tools you already know.

questions.prompt: Why check the exit code of a command you ran from Python?
options: Because the command can fail while your script carries on regardless
questions.explanation: Ignoring the exit code is how a script reports success after everything failed.

questions.prompt: Why read Terraform outputs rather than hardcoding the same values?
options: Because the values change when the infrastructure changes
questions.explanation: Hardcoded identifiers go stale the first time you rebuild an environment.

questions.prompt: What does producing a Terraform plan in JSON allow?
options: A program can analyse the proposed changes
questions.explanation: It turns a human readable plan into something you can write checks against.

questions.prompt: Why write a script that flags planned destroys?
options: Because a destroy hidden in a large plan is easy to miss
questions.explanation: This is the reviewer problem from day 150 of the DevOps track, automated.

questions.prompt: Why detect which environment a script is pointed at?
options: So a tool cannot act on production when you meant staging
questions.explanation: Wrong environment is one of the most damaging and most preventable mistakes.

questions.prompt: How should a destructive helper behave against production?
options: Refuse unless an explicit flag is given
questions.explanation: Friction in exactly the right place is what prevents the expensive accident.

questions.prompt: Why log the account and region at the start of a run?
options: So there is never ambiguity about what the script acted on
questions.explanation: When something goes wrong, the first question is always which account.

questions.prompt: What must a workflow do before running your Python script?
questions.explanation: Runners start clean, exactly as they did for your other pipeline steps.

questions.prompt: Why run a Python script in CI rather than on your laptop?
options: So it runs automatically and consistently rather than when you remember
questions.explanation: Anything that depends on you remembering will eventually be forgotten.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of a script that runs commands built from user input?
options: Unsafe input can cause unintended commands to run
questions.explanation: Passing arguments as a list rather than a single string is the safer habit.

questions.prompt: Why is this month lighter at the start?
options: Because it falls at the end of Ramadan and around Eid
questions.explanation: Both tracks reduce together, so no date has one full and one light course.

questions.prompt: A command that fails silently inside a Python script is a real risk.
questions.explanation: Without checking the exit code, your script reports success it did not achieve.

questions.prompt: Analysing a Terraform plan programmatically is a reasonable way to catch dangerous changes.
questions.explanation: It automates the review habit you built manually in the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: Hardcoding resource identifiers is acceptable if you only have one environment.
questions.explanation: One environment becomes two, and rebuilds change identifiers even when the count does not.

questions.prompt: What permissions should a scheduled audit workflow have?
options: Read only, scoped to what the audit reads
questions.explanation: An audit never needs to change anything, so it should not be able to.

questions.prompt: Why make the workflow fail on a high severity finding?
options: So the problem is visible rather than buried in a log nobody opens
questions.explanation: A report that nobody reads is the same as no report.

questions.prompt: Why save findings as a workflow artifact?
options: So you can download and analyse the full results later
questions.explanation: Logs get truncated and rotated, and an artifact keeps the full record.

questions.prompt: Why keep normal output clean and put detail behind a verbose flag?
options: Because a wall of detail makes the important result harder to see
questions.explanation: The default should serve the common case, not the debugging case.

questions.prompt: Where should a webhook URL come from?
options: An environment variable or secret store
questions.explanation: A webhook URL is a credential, and anyone with it can post as you.

questions.prompt: Why notify only when findings appear?
options: Because a message on every clean run trains people to ignore all of them
questions.explanation: The same alert noise problem you met with CloudWatch alarms.

questions.prompt: What does a Lambda handler receive?
options: An event and a context object
questions.explanation: The event describes what triggered it, and your code decides what to do with it.

questions.prompt: Why call the handler directly in a test?
options: So you can test the logic without deploying anything
questions.explanation: Deploy to test is a slow loop, and testing locally keeps you moving.

questions.prompt: Why does a Lambda need its dependencies packaged with it?
options: Because the runtime has no access to your local virtual environment
questions.explanation: It is the same reproducibility problem containers solve, in a different shape.

questions.prompt: What permissions should a Lambda's execution role have?
options: Only what the function actually needs
questions.explanation: Least privilege applies to automation exactly as it does to people.

questions.prompt: Why use logging rather than print inside a Lambda?
options: Because levels and structure make CloudWatch logs far more useful
questions.explanation: You will be debugging entirely from logs, so their quality matters more than usual.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of a scheduled function over a scheduled workflow?
options: It runs independently of your repository and its runners
questions.explanation: Each has a place, and knowing why you chose one is what matters.

questions.prompt: A notification sent on every successful run will eventually be ignored.
questions.explanation: It is the same reason you were told to delete alerts you would not act on.

questions.prompt: Testing a Lambda handler locally with a fake event is a reasonable substitute for some deployments.
questions.explanation: It shortens the feedback loop enormously while you are still shaping the logic.

questions.prompt: A webhook URL is harmless to commit because it is not a password.
questions.explanation: Anyone holding it can post messages as your integration, so it is a credential.

questions.prompt: Why write each report to S3 with a timestamped key?
options: So you build a history rather than overwriting the previous result
questions.explanation: The history is what lets you compare runs and see trends.

questions.prompt: Why report only what changed since the last run?
options: Because a full list every time hides the new problems among the old ones
questions.explanation: New findings are the actionable ones, and the rest are already known.

questions.prompt: Why fetch a secret once per run rather than on every call?
options: Because repeated calls add latency and can hit rate limits
questions.explanation: Caching within a single run is the sensible middle ground.

questions.prompt: Why check that no code path logs a secret?
options: Because error handling often prints values that were never meant to be visible
questions.explanation: The exception handler is the most common place a secret leaks by accident.

questions.prompt: What does idempotent mean for an automation?
options: Running it twice causes no additional effect
questions.explanation: Automation reruns, and anything that duplicates on a second run will eventually cause damage.

questions.prompt: Why prove idempotency by actually running twice?
options: Because assuming it is safe is how duplicate records appear in production
questions.explanation: The claim is cheap and the test is what makes it real.

questions.prompt: Why should a function catch its own failures rather than dying?
options: So the failure is reported rather than silent
questions.explanation: A crashed scheduled job produces no output at all, which nobody notices.

questions.prompt: Why create an alarm on function errors?
options: Because otherwise a broken schedule can fail for weeks unnoticed
questions.explanation: Scheduled automation fails silently by nature, so it needs explicit monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why trigger the error alarm on purpose?
options: To confirm it actually fires and reaches you
questions.explanation: An untested alarm is an assumption, and it fails on the day it matters.

questions.prompt: How should a tool handle three checks succeeding and one failing?
options: Report the successful results and the failure separately
questions.explanation: Throwing away good results because one check broke wastes the whole run.

questions.prompt: Why compare against a previous report rather than only reading the current one?
options: Because a trend tells you more than a snapshot
questions.explanation: Getting worse and getting better look identical in a single snapshot.

questions.prompt: What is the most common failure mode of scheduled automation?
options: It stops working and nobody notices
questions.explanation: Silence looks identical to everything being fine, which is why alarms matter.

questions.prompt: Scheduled automation needs monitoring more than interactive scripts do.
questions.explanation: Nobody is watching it run, so failure is invisible unless you make it visible.

questions.prompt: Error handling code is a common place for secrets to leak into logs.
questions.explanation: Printing the whole context on failure is a habit that quietly exposes credentials.

questions.prompt: An automation that duplicates records on a second run is acceptable if it rarely runs twice.
questions.explanation: Retries, manual reruns and overlapping schedules all happen, usually at the worst moment.

questions.prompt: What does defining an entry point give your tool?
options: It runs as a named command instead of a file path
questions.explanation: It is the difference between a script you remember the path to and a tool you install.

questions.prompt: Why declare dependencies in a project file?
options: So installation brings everything needed automatically
questions.explanation: The same reproducibility principle as requirements files and pinned images.

questions.prompt: Why install your own tool into a fresh environment?
options: Because it proves the packaging works for someone who is not you
questions.explanation: The same clean machine test you applied to your infrastructure repositories.

questions.prompt: What makes a good error message?
options: It says what went wrong and what to do about it
questions.explanation: The reader needs a next action, not just a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Why set defaults so the common use needs no flags?
options: Because a tool that needs six flags to do anything goes unused
questions.explanation: Convenience decides whether you actually run your own tools.

questions.prompt: Why run tests on every push to your own project?
options: So a change that breaks something is caught immediately
questions.explanation: The value of a test appears when you change something months later.

questions.prompt: Why add a linting step that fails the build?
options: Because most lint findings are real problems, and a warning nobody reads has no effect
questions.explanation: The same reasoning as failing the build on high severity scan findings.

questions.prompt: Why include example output in your README?
options: So a reader knows what to expect before running anything
questions.explanation: Showing the output answers half the questions a reader would otherwise ask.

questions.prompt: What should a usage example show?
options: The two or three ways the tool is actually used
questions.explanation: Exhaustive documentation goes unread, and a few real examples get used.

questions.prompt: Why review what you cannot rewrite unaided?
options: Because it separates what you completed from what you retained
questions.explanation: The same retention principle that appears again in Month 9.

questions.prompt: What does a packaged, tested, documented tool demonstrate?
options: That you can produce something another person could actually use
questions.explanation: Producing usable software is a different skill from writing working code.

questions.prompt: What has this month changed about your Python?
options: It moved from scripts you run to automation that runs itself
questions.explanation: Scheduled, monitored, packaged automation is a meaningfully different level.

questions.prompt: A tool that only you can install and run is only half finished.
questions.explanation: The packaging and documentation are what make it usable by anyone else.

questions.prompt: An error message that says what to do next is more useful than one that names the exception.
questions.explanation: The exception is for you, and the instruction is for whoever is running it.

questions.prompt: Running your own project's tests in CI is unnecessary for a small personal tool.
questions.explanation: Small tools grow, and the habit is what you are actually building this month.
